messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl and the Group,

I am a little confused one how the thresholds for the 'two QTL scan' were determined as 6.0, 4.7, 4.4, 4.7, 2.6 for mouse backcross (using the hyper data) at 5% significance for Tf, Ta, Ti, Tfv1, Tav1.

I am unclear what is meant by the  following text in your book (in Bold);
<These are estimated 95th percentiles of the null distributions of the corresponding LOD scores, obtained by 10,000 simulations of crosses with 250 individuals, markers at 10cM spacing and by hale-knott regression>

Please could you clarify 'simulations', is this the same as permutations (i.e reshuffling genotype and phenotype data to determine the likelihood of the LOD values occurring by chance in the genome).  Could you clarify if 'sim.cross' or 'operm' object of scanoneperm class were used? What are the main differences or benefits of one over the other in the application of two QTL mapping.  If permutations was applied then was stratified permutations approach used for the selective genotyped data in Hyper?

Secondly, simulations of crosses; what is meant by crosses?.

I would appreciate  any information regarding these thresholds and whether they can be applied to my study which aims to search for mouse modifiers in a backcross (n=143 and n=111 (irradiated and sham-irradiated groups) with 112 codominant markers (average genotype spacing of 14cM).

Thank you for you help.

Kind regards,

Eiram

messages.subject: Re: Two QTL scans
messages.body_plain:
It would be best to do proper permutation tests with your specific data.

Those thresholds were generated by simply simulating genotype data and then independent normally distributed phenotypes, running scantwo(), repeating many times, and calculating the 95th percentiles of the maximum LOD scores.

In place of a permutation test, you could just take your genotype data as given and simulate independent normally distributed phenotypes.  You'd be taking account of the particular marker density and pattern of missing genotype data.  The advantage of the permutation test is that you are also taking account of the specific oddities in the observed phenotypes.

In the simulation-based thresholds you ask about, I was using idealized genotype data, with evenly spaced markers with no missing data.  They may be reasonable rough guidelines, but it'd be better to derive your own thresholds.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl and group

I am trying to run scanone on a dataset with 3 phenotypes, and I am getting an error:

>malpheno<-scanone(aartest, pheno.col=2)

Error in checkcovar(cross, pheno.col, addcovar, intcovar, perm.strata,  :

  Following phenotypes are not numeric: Column 1

I get the same error when I specify any of the “real” phenotype columns with pheno.col (1, 2 or 3 - the 4th column is the ID and this is not numeric).

I have been trying to work out why with no success. I have run scanone before on different (but similar) phenotype data (same genotype data) with no problems, although in this case the phenotypes came in an excel file from a colleague. I checked the excel file and the cells are just the number, nothing else e.g. no calculations etc. I’m struggling to find out what the problem here might be, so I’m hoping someone can help.

I remembered a similar problem coming up in the discussion group before and looked it up.  Karl had suggested a check to see if the phenotypes were numeric, which I ran and got this output:

> which(!sapply(aartest$pheno, is.numeric))

Neal_Com   Neal_Mal  Neal_Gam   ID

       1          2         3    4

I think this means that the phenotype columns are not being read as numbers (is that correct?). I am not sure why this would be.

Here is the first line of the phenotype data:

> pull.pheno(aartest)

   Neal_Com Neal_Mal Neal_Gam     ID

1      2.69     0.27     2.82   3BB5

Some of these phenotypes are decimals rather than whole numbers – although I can’t see that is the problem as examples given in the help pages/ Karl’s wonderful book include decimals.

Many thanks for any ideas or suggestions.

Lisa

messages.body_plain:
In your data file, you should include some missing value code (like "NA" or "-") in cells with missing data, and then indicate the missing value code through the na.strings argument to read.cross().

My guess is that you have spaces or some other invisible text in such cells, and so the whole column is being interpreted as non-numeric.

Removing the individuals with missing data won't fix the problem, unless you do that to the file and then re-load the data.

A quick fix would be to just force them to be numeric

  for(i in 1:nphe(aartest))
    aartest$pheno[,i] <- as.numeric( as.character( aartest$pheno[,i] ) )

karl

messages.body_plain:
Dear Elisa,

Having seen your data and thought about this a bit more, it seems that you can just treat this as a standard backcross....just load the data with the argument genotypes=c("1", "3")

All offspring get a fixed chromosome from the inbred parent (AA) and a recombinant chromosome from the outbred parent (CD).  The key is to have inferred phase in that outbred parent.  But once you've done so, the offspring have genotypes AC or AD at any position, and it can be treated the same as the usual backcross.

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] multiple testing correction for multiple trait
messages.body_plain:
You should consider the number of traits analyzed when assessing QTL mapping results, but formal correction for the multiple phenotypes is seldom applied, and there's no standard method for doing so.

The following paper is an example of one approach I took:

Burrage LC, Baskin-Hill AE, Sinasac DS, Singer JB, Croniger CM, Kirby A, Kulbokas EJ, Daly MJ, Lander ES, Broman KW, Nadeau JH (2010) Genetic resistance to diet-induced obesity in chromosome substitution strains of mice. Mamm Genome 21:115-129

  http://www.biostat.wisc.edu/~kbroman/publications/burrage.pdf

karl
